english_translation: Let us start now before our time is taken up by other things.

dialogue.shona: Ngatitangei zvino tisati tapedzerwa nguva nezvimwe zvinhu.
dialogue.english: Let us start now before our time is taken up by other things.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ngatitangei [ngatitangei] • zvino [things no] • tisati [tisati] • tapedzerwa [tapedzerwa] • nguva [nguva] • nezvimwe [and / with zvimwe] • zvinhu [things nhu]

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nezvimwe'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nezvimwe'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'zvimwe' forms 'nezvimwe'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'tapedzerwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'tapedzerwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.

cultural_notes.title: Valuing Time ('Nguva') & Collective Initiative ('Ngatitangei!')
cultural_notes.content: Using the inclusive exhortative prefix 'Nga-ti-...-i' ('Ngatitangei!'—'Let us begin right now!') rallies a group to make the most of the morning hours before other duties demand attention.

active_exercises.prompt: You want to politely ask an elder or a group of guests to sit down ('gara'). Which imperative form should you use?
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' to the verb stem ('gara' -> 'garai') forms the plural and polite command in Shona.

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?
Choose the right locative prefix: You want to say 'The keys are ON the table' ('______tafura').
active_exercises.explanation: The prefix 'pa-' means 'on / at a specific surface', so 'pa-' + 'tafura' = 'patafura' ('on the table').
